name: Palmer v. Whitfield Industries
facts:
Lisa Palmer, a software engineer, signed a non-compete agreement with Whitfield Industries upon hire. The agreement barred her from working for any competing technology company within 100 miles for two years after separation. Palmer resigned after three years and accepted a position with a rival firm located 30 miles away. Whitfield sought a preliminary injunction.

The trial court granted the injunction, finding the agreement enforceable. Palmer appealed, arguing the geographic scope was unreasonable given that her role involved no client-facing responsibilities and her knowledge was limited to internal tools.
holding: Reversed. The Court of Appeals held that a 100-mile geographic restriction was unreasonable where the employee's role did not involve client relationships extending beyond the immediate metropolitan area. The court applied the three-factor reasonableness test under Franklin Rev. Stat. § 542.330 and found the geographic scope bore no reasonable relationship to the employer's legitimate business interest in protecting client relationships.
reasoning:
The court emphasized that geographic restrictions must be tailored to the actual scope of the employee's duties and the employer's protectable interests. 'A blanket geographic restriction that sweeps in territory where the employer has no clients, and where the employee had no contacts, is per se unreasonable.' The court noted that Palmer's work was entirely internal and that Whitfield failed to demonstrate any client relationship within the restricted area that Palmer could exploit.

The court distinguished Monroe v. TechStar Corp. on the ground that the employee in Monroe had direct access to trade secrets and client lists justifying a broader restriction.

name: Garner v. BioSynth Corp.
facts: Dr. Rachel Garner, a research chemist, left BioSynth Corp. to join a competitor. BioSynth sought to enforce a non-compete that prohibited Garner from working in pharmaceutical research within the state for one year. Garner argued the restriction was overbroad because it covered all pharmaceutical research, not just the specific compounds she worked on.
holding: The Supreme Court of Franklin held that employers must demonstrate a 'legitimate business interest' to enforce a non-compete under § 542.330(1)(a). A blanket prohibition on all work in an industry is unreasonable when the employer's protectable interest is limited to specific proprietary knowledge. However, the court upheld a narrower restriction preventing Garner from working on the specific compound class she researched at BioSynth.
reasoning:
The court established the framework that Franklin courts must follow: first, identify the employer's specific legitimate business interest (trade secrets, client relationships, or specialized training). Second, assess whether the restriction is no broader than necessary to protect that interest. The court stated: 'Non-compete agreements are restraints on trade and must be narrowly construed. The employer bears the burden of demonstrating that each element of the restriction — duration, geography, and scope of activity — is reasonably necessary to protect a legitimate interest.'

This case is the leading Franklin authority on the 'legitimate business interest' requirement.

name: Monroe v. TechStar Corp.
facts: David Monroe was a senior account manager at TechStar Corp. who had direct access to proprietary client lists, pricing strategies, and pending contract negotiations. His non-compete prohibited work for a competitor within 40 miles for 18 months. Monroe left to start his own consulting firm targeting TechStar's clients.
holding: The Court of Appeals upheld the non-compete as enforceable. The 40-mile radius and 18-month duration were reasonable in light of Monroe's extensive access to trade secrets and client relationships. The court granted TechStar's request for a preliminary injunction.
reasoning:
The court found all three prongs of the § 542.330 reasonableness test satisfied. Monroe had access to confidential pricing data and client strategies that could cause immediate competitive harm. The geographic scope matched TechStar's actual service area, and 18 months was reasonable to allow the information to become stale.

The court emphasized the distinction between employees with access to confidential information and those without: 'Where an employee has been entrusted with the employer's most sensitive competitive intelligence, courts must give meaningful effect to contractual protections that are otherwise reasonable in scope.'

name: Vasquez v. Pinnacle Data Solutions
facts: Maria Vasquez, a data analyst at Pinnacle Data Solutions (a marketing analytics firm), signed a non-compete barring her from working for any 'competing business' for one year within 30 miles. Vasquez left to join a healthcare data company. Pinnacle argued the healthcare company was a 'competing business' because both performed data analysis.
holding: The Court of Appeals held the non-compete unenforceable as applied. When the former employee's new role serves a fundamentally different industry and client base, the employer cannot demonstrate that the new position threatens a legitimate business interest. A company's interest in protecting client relationships and competitive intelligence does not extend to unrelated market segments.
reasoning:
The court held that 'competing business' must be construed narrowly in light of the employer's actual business: 'A marketing analytics firm and a healthcare data company may both analyze data, but they serve entirely different markets, clients, and regulatory environments. To hold that any company employing data analysts competes with any other is to render the employee effectively unemployable — a result § 542.330 was designed to prevent.'

The court cited Palmer v. Whitfield Industries for the principle that restrictions must be tailored to actual competitive harm, and Garner v. BioSynth Corp. for the requirement that employers identify specific protectable interests. The court distinguished Monroe v. TechStar Corp. because Monroe had targeted his former employer's actual clients.

name: Torres v. DataVault Inc.
facts: Elena Torres signed a non-compete with DataVault Inc. restricting her from working for a competitor within 60 miles for two years. The 60-mile radius encompassed the entire Greater Columbia metropolitan area — the only significant job market in the region for her specialty (database administration). Torres left DataVault and accepted a position with a competitor 15 miles away.
holding: The Columbia Court of Appeals struck down the non-compete as unreasonable. A geographic restriction that encompasses the employee's entire practical job market is effectively a blanket prohibition on employment in the field and violates public policy.
reasoning:
The court reasoned: 'When a geographic restriction renders an employee effectively unable to practice her profession anywhere within commuting distance, the restriction has exceeded any legitimate protective purpose and becomes a punitive restraint on livelihood. Courts must consider the practical geography of the employee's job market, not merely draw circles on a map.'

Though this is a Columbia case and not binding in Franklin, the court's reasoning on metropolitan-area restrictions is persuasive. The court noted a growing national trend toward scrutinizing geographic restrictions in knowledge-economy employment.

name: Henderson v. Apex Financial Group
facts: James Henderson was a financial advisor at Apex Financial Group who personally managed relationships with over 200 high-net-worth clients. His non-compete prohibited him from soliciting Apex clients for two years within 25 miles. Henderson left and immediately contacted his former clients to move their accounts.
holding: The court upheld the non-compete, finding that Henderson's deep personal client relationships constituted a legitimate business interest justifying the restriction. The 25-mile radius and two-year duration were reasonable given the nature of the client relationships.
reasoning:
The court focused on the value of client relationships in the financial advisory context: 'Where the employee is the face of the business to the client, the employer's investment in cultivating those relationships is a protectable interest of the highest order.' The court found Henderson's immediate solicitation of clients demonstrated exactly the competitive harm the non-compete was designed to prevent.

This case is factually distinguishable from situations where the employee had no direct client contact or where the clients were not transferable.

name: Blackwell v. Orion Systems
facts: Karen Blackwell was a project manager at Orion Systems who had access to client lists, project pricing models, and staffing strategies. She signed a non-compete barring work for competitors within 50 miles for 18 months. Blackwell resigned and joined a competitor, though she did not bring any documents or solicit Orion's clients.
holding: The court upheld the non-compete. Even though Blackwell did not actively misappropriate information, her knowledge of Orion's pricing strategies and client needs was itself a protectable interest. The 50-mile, 18-month restriction was reasonable given her level of access.
reasoning:
The court applied the three-factor test from Garner v. BioSynth Corp. and found each element reasonable. On the question of whether mere knowledge (without active misappropriation) could justify enforcement, the court stated: 'The purpose of a non-compete is prophylactic — it prevents the risk of disclosure, not merely actual disclosure. An employee who carries proprietary knowledge to a competitor poses an inherent risk to the former employer, even with the best of intentions.'

The court cited Henderson v. Apex Financial Group for the principle that client-relationship knowledge is independently protectable. The court noted that its ruling 'should not be read to validate restrictions where the employee had no meaningful access to confidential information or client relationships.'

name: Whitmore v. Sterling & Associates
facts: Thomas Whitmore, an attorney, signed a non-compete prohibiting him from practicing law within 100 miles for five years. The law firm sought enforcement. Whitmore argued the restriction was unreasonable in both duration and geographic scope.
holding: The court found the restriction unreasonable but reformed ('blue-penciled') it to a 25-mile, one-year restriction rather than voiding it entirely. Franklin follows the blue-pencil doctrine, allowing courts to narrow overbroad restrictions to reasonable terms.
reasoning:
The court acknowledged that the original terms were 'plainly unreasonable' but held that the strong public policy favoring freedom of contract supported reformation rather than voiding. The court cautioned, however, that 'the blue-pencil doctrine is not an invitation for employers to draft extravagant restrictions in the hope that courts will reduce them to something reasonable. Employers who consistently overreach risk having their agreements voided entirely.'

Note: This case's precedential value is limited — the Franklin legislature subsequently amended § 542.330 in 2015 to add subsection (3), which restricts judicial reformation. See statute_01.

name: Nakamura v. Vertex Analytics
facts: Dr. Kenji Nakamura was a data scientist at Vertex Analytics. His non-compete barred competing work for 24 months. Nakamura argued that in the fast-moving data science field, any confidential knowledge he had would be obsolete within months. Vertex countered that its client relationships, not just technical knowledge, justified the full two-year term.
holding: The court found 24 months unreasonable and reduced the enforceable period to 12 months. In technology fields where information depreciates rapidly, temporal restrictions must account for the shelf life of the protectable interest.
reasoning:
The court held: 'In an industry where methodologies, tools, and market conditions change in months rather than years, a two-year restriction protects yesterday's secrets at the cost of tomorrow's livelihood. Temporal reasonableness under § 542.330(1)(c) requires courts to consider the rate at which the protectable information loses its competitive value.'

The court distinguished traditional industries (law, finance, manufacturing) where client relationships may justify longer restrictions from technology sectors where the competitive advantage of confidential information decays rapidly.

name: Chen v. Ridgeline Technologies
facts: Wei Chen left Ridgeline Technologies to start his own cybersecurity consultancy. Ridgeline sought a preliminary injunction under Chen's non-compete. Chen's new firm targeted small businesses; Ridgeline served enterprise clients exclusively. Ridgeline had not lost any clients and could not identify any specific competitive harm caused by Chen's departure.
holding: The court denied the preliminary injunction. An employer seeking to enforce a non-compete must demonstrate actual or imminent competitive harm, not merely theoretical risk. Where the employer cannot show any lost clients, diverted business, or misuse of confidential information, enforcement is unwarranted.
reasoning:
The court stated: 'A non-compete agreement is not a property right entitling the employer to enjoin any subsequent employment. It is a contractual tool for preventing specific competitive harm. Where the employer identifies no harm — no lost clients, no diverted contracts, no evidence of confidential information misuse — the agreement lacks the factual predicate for enforcement.'

The court cited Palmer v. Whitfield Industries and Garner v. BioSynth Corp. for the principle that restrictions must map to actual protectable interests, not hypothetical ones.

name: Foster v. Greystone Management
facts: Rebecca Foster challenged a non-compete with a 200-mile radius and three-year duration. Greystone Management asked the court to blue-pencil the agreement to reasonable terms, as had been done in Whitmore v. Sterling & Associates.
holding: The court declined to reform the agreement. Under the 2015 amendment to § 542.330, subsection (3) now limits judicial reformation to cases where the original terms were 'not unreasonable on their face.' A 200-mile, three-year restriction was facially unreasonable, and the court voided the entire non-compete rather than rewriting it.
reasoning:
The court found that the 2015 amendment signaled a legislative shift: 'The legislature amended § 542.330 specifically to curtail the blue-pencil doctrine. Employers can no longer draft egregiously overbroad agreements and rely on courts to fix them. Where the original terms are facially unreasonable — as a 200-mile, three-year restriction plainly is — the court must void the agreement, not rescue it.'

The court noted that Whitmore v. Sterling, decided before the amendment, would likely come out differently under current law. This case is significant for any scenario where the employer's restriction is arguably overbroad.

name: Richardson v. Lake City Hospital
facts: Dr. Samuel Richardson, a cardiologist, signed a non-compete with Lake City Hospital prohibiting him from practicing within 30 miles for two years. The 30-mile radius was the only area within 100 miles with a cardiology practice. Richardson argued the restriction was unduly burdensome and contrary to public interest in healthcare access.
holding: The court struck down the non-compete, holding that the 'undue burden' prong of § 542.330(1)(d) requires consideration of both the burden on the employee and the impact on the public. Where a restriction would deprive a community of needed services, it is unenforceable regardless of the employer's legitimate interest.
reasoning:
The court stated: 'The reasonableness inquiry under § 542.330 does not occur in a vacuum. Subsection (1)(d) expressly requires that the agreement not be unduly burdensome to the employee, and we hold that this inquiry necessarily encompasses the broader public interest. A non-compete that would remove the only specialist from an underserved area imposes a burden that no private commercial interest can justify.'

While this case involves healthcare specifically, its reasoning about the 'undue burden' prong applies to any situation where a restriction effectively bars the employee from their profession.

name: Wagner v. CompuTech Services
facts: Paul Wagner signed a non-compete two years into his at-will employment at CompuTech Services. He received no raise, bonus, or other new consideration at the time of signing. When he later left for a competitor, CompuTech sought enforcement.
holding: The court held the non-compete unenforceable for lack of consideration. Continued at-will employment alone is insufficient consideration for a new restrictive covenant in Franklin. The employer must provide independent consideration — such as a raise, promotion, bonus, or access to new confidential information.
reasoning: The court reasoned: 'An at-will employee who is told to sign a non-compete or face termination has not freely bargained for a restriction on future employment. Where no new consideration flows to the employee, the agreement is illusory. We join the majority of jurisdictions holding that continued employment, standing alone, cannot support a covenant not to compete entered into after the employment relationship has begun.'
